articles.title: What Should You Hand To an AI?
articles.excerpt: A free app I built myself. Give it a try. You asked an AI to do the same job ten times and got ten slightly different results. That job does not belong to the AI. AI is good at judgement; programs are…
articles.body: A free app I built myself. Give it a try. You asked an AI to do the same job ten times and got ten slightly different results. That job does not belong to the AI. AI is good at judgement; programs are good at repetition. This post gives one test that separates the two. It also shows what to do with the work that lands on the program side. There is one test - can the answer be fixed by a rule? Say the same input must always give the same answer. If you can write that answer down as a rule, it is a program. If the input differs every time and the answer depends on context, it is AI. That sounds abstract.
articles.author: DroidActor Dotori

articles.body: If you want the words spoken in 500 TikTok videos, the obvious plan is to download each video and run it through Whisper. It works, and it is wasteful: a large share of TikTok videos already have a transcript sitting in the page, generated by TikTok itself. This post walks through where those captions live, the traps in picking the right track, and when you actually need speech-to-text. I ended up building this into an Apify actor, which I link at the end. Disclosure: I am the developer. Where TikTok keeps its captions Load a public video page, for example https://www.tiktok.com/@nasa/video/7707774305056083213 , and look at the HTML. articles.title: The Technical Book That Changed Because You Did
articles.excerpt: Disclosure: The author is affiliated with 365NanoBook, a book-summary program mentioned as one example in this article. I read Robert Martin's Clean Code for the first time about a year into my first…
articles.body: Disclosure: The author is affiliated with 365NanoBook, a book-summary program mentioned as one example in this article. I read Robert Martin's Clean Code for the first time about a year into my first real job, mostly because a senior engineer I admired kept quoting it in code reviews. I finished it in a weekend, nodded along, and put it on the shelf feeling like I had absorbed it. I had not absorbed it. I had only finished it, and early in a career those feel like the same thing. I read it again six years later, after shipping a service I had designed myself and then spending three months debugging it at 2 a.m. The book was the same. The chapters were the same. The code examples were the same. But the reading was unrecognizable.

articles.title: Workday career sites stop at 2,000 jobs. Here is how to get all of them.
articles.excerpt: I build data tools on Apify, and one of the first requests I kept seeing was simple: "I want every open job from Company X's Workday site." It sounds like a 30-line script. It is, right up until the c…
articles.body: I build data tools on Apify, and one of the first requests I kept seeing was simple: "I want every open job from Company X's Workday site." It sounds like a 30-line script. It is, right up until the company has more than 2,000 openings. This post explains the 2,000 cap, why paging cannot get past it, and the approach I ended up shipping: split the search by Workday's own filters until every slice is small enough, then merge and dedupe. At the end there is a hosted version you can call from Python if you do not want to maintain it yourself. Disclosure up front: I built that actor. The Workday jobs API in two minutes Every career site on *.myworkdayjobs.com is a single-page app backed by a JSON endpoint.

articles.excerpt: Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its stellar companion.
articles.body: Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a new study reports. As stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby. In a binary star system, this can include a dying star merging with its companion star. However, scientists had never directly seen any examples of such a cosmic drama unfolding — until now. "Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in New York, told Space.com. "When a star engulfs its companion, its effect is very subtle — like throwing a bucket of water in a large ocean.

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 18, 2013: NASA launches MAVEN spacecraft to Mars to find out how the Red Planet lost its water
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 18, 2013, NASA launched the MAVEN spacecraft to Mars to investigate the planet's missing water. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 18, 2013, NASA launched the MAVEN spacecraft to Mars. The name of NASA's MAVEN spacecraft stands for Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN. The spacecraft was an orbiter designed to help scientists figure out what happened to the water on Mars and its atmosphere. Mars is dry today, but it data from several Mars missions suggest that it was a much wetter environment a long time ago. MAVEN tracked the rate of atmospheric loss from Mars . The planet has a super thin atmosphere that has been leaking into space for a few billion years. Scientists think that when Mars lost its atmosphere, water dried up on the surface as a result. Solar storms that blast radiation into the solar system appear to have blasted away some of the atmosphere.

articles.title: Earth is missing over a billion years of geological history. Scientists may have discovered why
articles.excerpt: The answer to one of Earth's greatest geological mysteries may lie deep beneath our feet.
articles.body: More than a billion years of Earth's history has seemingly vanished. Across the planet, ancient rock formations contain colossal gaps in the geological record, leaving scientists puzzled over what happened to the missing chapters of our planet's past. Now, researchers believe they may have found an explanation, and the answer lies deep inside Earth . Normally, layers of sediment build up over time, eventually forming sedimentary rocks that preserve clues about our planet's past. Older layers generally lie beneath younger ones, allowing geologists to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years. But the geological record isn't always so neatly arranged.
